title: Theorem
body_md:
Let \(S\) be a training dataset, \(M=\mathcal{A}(S)\),
\((\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{\bar{A}})\) satisfy \(\left({\alpha,\varepsilon}\right)\)-Rényi unlearning,
and \(U_1,\ldots,U_K\) be the unlearning requests. For each request,
let \(W_i=\mathcal{A}(S\setminus U_i)\) be the corresponding
retrained model. Then, for any ordering \(\pi\) of the requests,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(M;S)
\gtrsim{}&
\sum_{i=1}^K
H\!\left(
W_{\pi(i)}
\mid W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\leq i)}
\right)-
K\cdot\mathrm{err}(\alpha,\varepsilon).
\end{aligned}
\]

label: def:renyi-unlearning
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:renyi-unlearning}
Fix \(\alpha>1\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\). We say that
\(\left({\mathcal{A},\mathcal{\bar{A}}}\right)\) satisfies
\(\left({\alpha,\varepsilon}\right)\)-Rényi unlearning (RU) over deletion sets of
size at most \(m\) if, for every dataset \(S\in\cX^n\) and every
request \(U\subseteq S\) with \(|U|\leq m\),
\[
    d_\alpha\left({
        \mathcal{\bar{A}}\left({\mathcal{A}(S),U}\right),
        \mathcal{\bar{A}}\left({\mathcal{A}(S\setminus U),\emptyset}\right)
    }\right)
    \le \varepsilon .
\]
When \(m\) is clear from context, we simply say that
\(\left({\mathcal{A},\mathcal{\bar{A}}}\right)\) satisfies
\(\left({\alpha,\varepsilon}\right)\)-R\'enyi unlearning.

name: R\'enyi unlearning

label: def:gamma-utility
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:gamma-utility}
Fix a metric \(d_{\cW}\) on \(\cW\) and a non-increasing function
\(\Gamma:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]\). For each \(w\in\cW\), let
\(Q_w\coloneqq\mathrm{Law}(\mathcal{\bar{A}}(w,\emptyset))\). We say that \(\mathcal{\bar{A}}\)
has \((d_{\cW},\Gamma)\)-utility on empty requests if, for every
\(w\in\cW\) and every radius \(r\geq0\),
\[
    \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right)_{W^\emptyset\sim Q_w}
    \!\left[d_{\cW}(W^\emptyset,w)>r\right]\leq\Gamma(r).
\]

body_md:
\label{ex:gaussian-utility}

\(\mathcal{\bar{A}}(w,\emptyset)=w+Z\), where
\(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I_d)\). Then \(\mathcal{\bar{A}}\) has
\(\left({\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_2,\Gamma}\right)\)-utility with
\(\Gamma(r)=1\) for \(r<\sigma\sqrt d\), and

label: def:deletion-gap
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:deletion-gap}
Fix a learning algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\), a norm \(\phi\), integers
\(N\ge2\) and \(m\ge0\), and parameters \(\alpha>1\), \(\Delta>0\),
\(\delta_\alpha\ge0\), and \(\kappa\in[0,1]\).  We call
\((S_1,\ldots,S_N,U)\), with \(S_i\in\cX^n\), an
\((N,m,\Delta,\phi;\delta_\alpha,\kappa)\)-\emph{shared-deletion
example} (s.d.e.) for \(\mathcal{A}\) if:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item \(U\subseteq\bigcap_{i=1}^N S_i\) and \(|U|\le m\).

    \item For every distinct \(i,j\in[N]\),
    \(
        d_\alpha\bigl(\mathcal{A}(S_i),\mathcal{A}(S_j)\bigr)
        \le \delta_\alpha.
    \)

    \item There exist measurable sets \(E_1,\ldots,E_N\subseteq\cW\)
    such that, for every distinct \(i,j\in[N]\),
    \(
        \phi(x-z)\ge\Delta\) for all \(x\in E_i,\ z\in E_j,
    \)
    and, for every \(i\in[N]\),
    \(
        \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right)_{W\sim\mathcal{A}(S_i\setminus U)}[W\in E_i]
        \ge 1-\kappa.
    \)
\end{enumerate}

label: thm:concentration-impossibility
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first $\delta_\alpha = 0$. Write $W_i \coloneqq \mathcal{A}(S_i
\setminus U)$ and $Q_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Law}(\mathcal{\bar{A}}(W_i, \emptyset))$.
Since $\mathcal{A}(S_i)$ has the same law for all $i$ and $\mathcal{\bar{A}}$
is forget-only, all $N$ deletion requests have the same output law $T
\coloneqq \mathrm{Law}(\mathcal{\bar{A}}(M, U))$, $M \sim \mathrm{Law}\left({\mathcal{A}(S_1)}\right)$, and the
unlearning guarantee gives $ 
  D_{\IfNoValueTF{Q_i\,\|\,T}{\alpha}{Q_i\,\|\,T}}\!\left( \le \right) 
 \varepsilon$ and
$ 
  D_{\IfNoValueTF{T\,\|\,Q_i}{\alpha}{T\,\|\,Q_i}}\!\left( \le \right) 
 \varepsilon$ for every $i$.

Fix $r \in (0, \Delta/2)$ with $0 < u(r) < 1$. By the separation
property of shared deletion examples (property $(3)$) and
\Cref{lem:renyi-from-concentration}, there are disjoint sets $B_i$
with $Q_i(B_i) \ge 1 - u(r)$ such that each retraining target
concentrates on its own set, yet the single law $T$ must stay close to
all of them.  Then, using the R\'enyi unlearning inequality (\Cref{lem:renyi-event-transfer}), we get
that \(T\) must give some probability mass to every \(B_i\):
\[
    1 - u(r) \le Q_i(B_i) \le e^{\gamma\varepsilon}\, T(B_i)^{\gamma}
    \implies
    T(B_i) \ge e^{-\varepsilon} \left({1 - u(r)}\right)^{1/\gamma}.
\]
However, since $T$ has only one unit of mass to share among the disjoint
sets:
\[
    1 \ge \sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N} T(B_i) \ge N e^{-\varepsilon} \left({1 - u(r)}\right)^{1/\gamma}
    \implies
    \varepsilon \ge \log N + \tfrac{1}{\gamma} \log\left({1 - u(r)}\right) .
\]
This is the first term of the maximum. The second follows from the same steps
applied to $B_i^c$ with $ 
  D_{\IfNoValueTF{T\,\|\,Q_i}{\alpha}{T\,\|\,Q_i}}\!\left( \le \right) 
 \varepsilon$, which forces $T$
to stay inside every $B_i$, giving $T(B_i) \ge 1 - e^{\gamma\varepsilon} u(r)^{\gamma}$.
Taking the supremum over $r$ gives the exact collision lower bound.

For $\delta_\alpha > 0$, the unlearned laws $T_i$ may differ, but data
processing gives $d_\alpha(T_i, T_1) \le \delta_\alpha$. Each estimate then
passes through $T_i$ first; this extra application
of~\Cref{lem:renyi-event-transfer} replaces $\gamma$ by $\gamma^2$ and adds the
$\delta_\alpha$ penalties in the approximate collision lower bound.

label: ex:svm
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:svm}
Fix dimension \(d\ge2\). Let \(\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}\) be the
hard-margin homogeneous linear SVM on realizable samples supported on
\(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\left\lVertx\right\rVert_2\le1\}\times\{-1,+1\}\). That is,
\(\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}\) returns the minimum-norm separator
\(w\) satisfying \(y\left\langle{w},{x}\right\rangle\ge1\) for all training examples
\((x,y)\). For every \(\Delta>0\), this learner admits a
\((2,1,\Delta,\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_2;0,0)\)-s.d.e.

The learner returns the unnormalized SVM vector, so its model
space is unbounded and the separation \(\Delta\) can be
arbitrarily large. If the learner instead returns the normalized
direction \(w/\left\lVertw\right\rVert_2\), the same construction gives a
\((2,1,\sqrt2,\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_2;0,0)\)-s.d.e.

label: pp:teaching-dimension
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pp:teaching-dimension}
    Fix \(N>1\) and let $\cH$ be a hypothesis class with finite
    teaching dimension $\tau$ and $|\cH| \geq N$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be
    any empirical risk minimizer for the zero-one loss, $\phi$ be any
    norm on a vector space containing $\cH$, and let $h_1,\dots,h_N
    \in \cH$ be distinct.  Then there exist $(S_1,\dots,S_N,U)$ with
    $|U| = O(\tau^2)$ and $|S_i| = o(\tau^3)$ for all $i \in [N]$ such
    that $\mathcal{A}(S_i) = \mathcal{A}(S_j)$ and $\mathcal{A}(S_i
    \setminus U) = h_i$ for all $i\neq j \in [N]$.  Consequently,
    $\mathcal{A}$ admits an
    \(
        (N, O(\tau^2), \Delta, \phi; 0, 0)
    \)-s.d.e. with $\Delta \coloneqq \min_{i \neq j} \phi(h_i - h_j)$.

title: Setup
body_md:
Draw
\(
    S \sim \mathcal{P}_S
\)
and allow $\mathcal{A}$ to be randomized.
The requests 
\(
    \mathcal{U} = \left\{{
        U_1, \dots, U_K
    }\right\}
\)
are deterministic functions of $S$, with $U_i \subseteq S$
\footnote{
    They can also be randomized; the distribution of $U_i$ must be independent of the algorithmic randomness.
}.
For each $i \in [K]$, define
\(
    M \coloneqq \mathcal{A}(S),
\)
\(
    W_i \coloneqq \mathcal{A}(S \setminus U_i),
\)
\(
    \overline{W}_i \coloneqq \mathcal{\bar{A}}(\mathcal{A}(S), U_i),
\)
\(
    W^\emptyset_i \coloneqq \mathcal{\bar{A}}(\mathcal{A}(S \setminus U_i), \emptyset).
\)
Thus, $M$ is the pretrained model, $W_i$ is the retraining target for the request $U_i$,
$\overline{W}_i$ is the unlearning output,
while $W^\emptyset_i$ is the empty-request output of $W_i$.
For a tuple
\(
    A^K \coloneqq \left({
        A_1, \dots, A_K
    }\right)
\)
and a permutation $\pi: [K] \mapsto [K]$,
write
\(
    A_{\pi(\leq i)}
    \coloneqq \left({
        A_{\pi(1)}, \dots, A_{\pi(i)}
    }\right)
\)
and
\(
    A_{\pi(< i)}
    \coloneqq \left({
        A_{\pi(1)}, \dots, A_{\pi(i-1)}
    }\right).
\)
When $i=1$, $A_{\pi(<1)}$ is the empty tuple.
\Cref{fig:markov-graph} records the conditional
independences used below: $M$ is independent of $(U_i, W_i)$ given $S$,
$\overline{W}_i$ depends on the rest only through $(M, U_i)$,
and $W^\emptyset_i$ depends only on $W_i$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Recall that $W = \mathcal{A}(S\setminus U)$ and $\overline W = \mathcal{\bar{A}}(M,U)$.
The \textit{unlearning recovery error} is
\[
    \beta_{\mathrm{un}} \coloneqq \sup_{\substack{s,u:\, u\subseteq s\\ |u|\le m}}
    \mathbb P\big(\overline W \ne W \mid S=s,\, U=u\big),
\]
where the probability is over the randomness of $\mathcal{A}$ and
$\mathcal{\bar{A}}$, with independent runs of $\mathcal{A}$ for fixed $s,u$.

label: lem:t-recovery-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:t-recovery-bound}
Assume that \((\mathcal{A},\mathcal{\bar{A}})\) satisfies
\(\left({\alpha,\varepsilon}\right)\)-R\'enyi unlearning for all deletion
requests of size at most \(m\) and \(\mathcal{\bar{A}}\) has
\((d_0,\Gamma)\)-utility on empty requests with \(\eta\coloneqq\Gamma(0)\).
Define \(\gamma\coloneqq\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\). Then,
\[
    \beta_{\mathrm{un}} \leq \bar{\beta}\coloneqq \min \left\{{1, e^{\gamma \varepsilon} 
    \left({\eta + \Delta_{\mathcal A}}\right)^\gamma}\right\}, \quad 
    \Delta_{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq \sup_{\substack{s,u:\,u\subseteq
    s\\ |u|\le m}} \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right){ W_{s,u}^{(1)}\ne W_{s,u}^{(2)} },
\]  
where \(W_{s,u}^{(1)}\) and \(W_{s,u}^{(2)}\) are independent runs of \(\mathcal{A}(s\setminus u)\).
head: environment

label: thm:information-lb-discrete
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:information-lb-discrete}
    Let $S \sim \cP_S$, and $U_1, \dots, U_K$ be a set of unlearning requests generated as above, each of size at most $m$. Assume $\mathcal{W}$ is finite and that $(\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{\bar{A}})$ satisfy the same assumptions as in \Cref{lem:t-recovery-bound}, with $\bar{\beta}$ as defined there. Set $\tilde{\beta} \coloneqq \min\left\{{\bar{\beta},\, 1 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{W}|}}\right\}$.  
    Then, for any permutation $\pi : [K] \to [K]$,
    \[
        I(M;S) \geq \sum_{i=1}^{K} H\left({W_{\pi(i)} \mid W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\le i)}}\right)
        - K\left({h(\tilde{\beta}) + \tilde{\beta}\log\left({|\mathcal{W}| - 1}\right)}\right),  
    \]
    where $h$ denotes the binary entropy.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply~\Cref{pp:information-lb}. It remains to lower bound each term
    $I(W_{\pi(i)};\overline W_{\pi(i)}\mid \cH_i)$, where
    $\cH_i \coloneqq (W_{\pi(<i)},U_{\pi(\le i)})$. Use the definition of mutual information and the fact that conditioning reduces entropy, to get
    $I(W_{\pi(i)};\overline W_{\pi(i)}\mid \cH_i)
    \ge H(W_{\pi(i)}\mid \cH_i) - H(W_{\pi(i)}\mid \overline W_{\pi(i)})$.
    \Cref{lem:t-recovery-bound} gives $\mathbb P(\overline W_{\pi(i)}\ne W_{\pi(i)})\le\bar\beta$, and
    Fano's inequality gives
    $H(W_{\pi(i)}\mid \overline W_{\pi(i)})\le h(\tilde\beta)+\tilde\beta\log(|\mathcal W|-1)$.
    Plugging this back into the mutual information bound and summing over $i$ proves the theorem.

title: Remark
body_md:
Since the Rényi unlearning guarantee holds for every dataset and every
    admissible deletion request, the memorization bound applies to any family of
    requests, up to the family of all nonempty subsets of $S$ of size at most $m$.
    Most of these requests, however, may not reveal new information about the retraining
    targets, while each still contributes a penalty term. In the examples below, we
    therefore choose a small family of requests, each revealing new information, so
    that $K$ is much smaller than the number of admissible requests.

label: pp:canonical-thresholds
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pp:canonical-thresholds}
    Let \(n\ge 2m\), let \(q\ge2\), and set \(N=nq\). Then there
    exists a distribution \(\cP_S\) over realizable threshold samples
    of size \(n\), and there are deletion requests \(U_1,\ldots,U_m\),
    each of size exactly \(m\), such that any forget-only unlearning
    algorithm satisfying the assumptions above must obey
    \[
        I(M;S) 
        \geq

            -
            \beta_q
            \log \left({

            }\right)
            -
            h(\beta_q)
        }\right].

    \(I(M;S)_{\mathrm{bare}}=\log\left({N/n}\right)\).

label: prop:factorized-matrix-completion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:factorized-matrix-completion}
    Let \(d>4\) be the ambient number of scalar matrix entries, let
    \(m\ge1\) be the deletion budget, and let \(n>3m\) be the dataset size.
    Define \(
        r_\star
        \coloneqq
        \min\left\{{ \left\lfloor\sqrt d\right\rfloor,
            \left\lfloor\frac{n}{m+1}\right\rfloor}\right\}.  \) Then there
            exists a distribution \(\cP_S\) over datasets of size \(n\),
            and deletion requests \(U_1,\ldots,U_{r_\star}\), each of

    \[
        I(M;S)
        \ge
        \log(r_\star!)
        -
        \sum_{s=2}^{r_\star}
        \left[{
            h(\beta_s) + \beta_s \log(s-1)}\right].

    \(I(M;S)_{\mathrm{bare}}=0\) when no unlearning is required.

title: Remark
body_md: We would like to highlight a consequence of our lower bounds, which can hold for a variety of algorithms. For instance, in the case of the canonical threshold ERM learner, the algorithm is simply outputting a real number - the threshold - from a finite set of possible thresholds. Unlearning, on the other hand, imposes the requirement to retain significantly more information than just this single number. However, there is no way to encode all of this additional information into that one number while remaining within the original model space. This implies that we may need to move to a different output space in order to output this additional information, and possibly design a different algorithm for the unlearning problem.

label: app:proof-concentration-impossibility
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{app:proof-concentration-impossibility}
    For $i \in [N]$, write 
    $M_i \coloneqq \mathcal{A}(S_i)$,
    $W_i \coloneqq \mathcal{A}(S_i \setminus U)$,
    $P_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Law}(W_i)$,
    $Q_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Law} (\mathcal{\bar{A}}(W_i, \emptyset))$,
    and $T_i \coloneqq \mathrm{Law}(\mathcal{\bar{A}}(M_i, U))$.
    Define
    \(
        B_i \coloneqq \left\{{
            w \in \cW: \;
            \left({
                \exists z \in E_i
            }\right)\quad
            \phi(w - z) \leq r
        }\right\},
    \)
    and $\gamma = \frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}$.
    
    Recall that $u(r) \coloneqq \kappa + \Gamma(r)$, and fix $r \in R$, so $0 < r < \Delta/2$ and $0 < u(r) < 1$.
    For each pair $i \neq j$, the sets $E_i, E_j$ from the
    shared deletion example satisfy
    \[
        \left({
            \forall z_i \in E_i
        }\right)
        \left({
            \forall z_j \in E_j
        }\right)
        \quad
        \phi( z_i - z_j ) \geq \Delta > 2r,
    \]
    and
    \(
        \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right)_{W_k \sim P_k} \left({W_k \in E_k}\right) \geq 1 - \kappa
    \)
    for $k \in \left\{{i, j}\right\}$.
    Applying~\Cref{lem:renyi-from-concentration} to the laws $P_i, P_j$ and the
    sets $E_i, E_j$, we get that $B_i \cap B_j = \emptyset$ and
    $Q_i(B_i) \geq 1 - u(r)$, implying $Q_i(B_i^c) \leq u(r)$.
    Since this holds for every pair $i \neq j$, the sets $B_1, \dots, B_N$ are
    pairwise disjoint.

    The unlearning assumption gives $d_\alpha (Q_i, T_i) \leq \varepsilon$ for all $i \in [N]$.
    As $T_i$ is the image of $M_i$ under the map $w \to \mathcal{\bar{A}}(w, U)$, by the data processing inequality, we have that, for $i \neq j$,
    \[
        d_\alpha(T_i, T_j) \leq d_\alpha(M_i, M_j) \leq \delta_\alpha.
    \]
    Specifically, we will use $d_\alpha(T_1, T_i) \leq \delta_\alpha$.

    As the sets $B_1, \dots, B_N$ are disjoint, it holds that,
    \(
        \sum_{i=1}^N T_1(B_i) \leq 1.
    \)

    We first analyze the exact collision case, which also covers the deterministic learners. The zero-collision condition forces $T_i = T_1$, which implies $d_\alpha(Q_i, T_1) \leq \varepsilon$ for all $i \in [N]$.
    Using~\Cref{lem:renyi-event-transfer} in two directions, together with the unlearning assumption, we have,
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        1 - u(r) \leq Q_i(B_i) \leq e^{\gamma \varepsilon} T_1(B_i)^\gamma
        &\implies
        T_1(B_i) \geq e^{-\varepsilon} \left({1 - u(r)}\right)^{1 / \gamma}, \\
        1 - T_1(B_i) = T_1(B_i^c) \leq e^{\gamma \varepsilon} Q_i(B_i^c)^\gamma \leq e^{\gamma \varepsilon} u(r)^\gamma
        &\implies
        T_1(B_i) \geq 1 - e^{\gamma \varepsilon} u(r)^\gamma
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Summing each lower bound over $i$ and using
    \(
        \sum_{i=1}^N T_1(B_i) \leq 1,
    \)
    we get the final two terms depending on $r$.

    In the approximate collision case, we use~\Cref{lem:renyi-event-transfer} twice to get,
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        &1 - u(r) 
        \leq Q_i(B_i) 
        \leq e^{\gamma \varepsilon} T_i(B_i)^\gamma
        \leq e^{\gamma \varepsilon + \gamma^2 \delta_\alpha} T_1(B_i)^{\gamma^2}
        \implies
        T_1 (B_i) \geq \left({
            1 - u(r)}\right)^{1 / \gamma^2}
         e^{-\varepsilon/\gamma - \delta_\alpha}, \\
        &T_1(B_i^c) 
        \leq e^{\gamma \delta_\alpha} T_i(B_i^c)^\gamma
        \leq e^{\gamma^2 \varepsilon + \gamma \delta_\alpha}
        Q_i(B_i^c)^{\gamma^2}
        \leq e^{\gamma^2 \varepsilon + \gamma \delta_\alpha} u(r)^{\gamma^2}
        \implies
        T_1(B_i) \geq 1 - e^{\gamma^2 \varepsilon + \gamma \delta_\alpha} u(r)^{\gamma^2},
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Here we used that $x \mapsto x^\gamma$ is increasing. Summing the first lower bound over the disjoint sets $B_i$ gives
    \[
        1 \geq \sum_{i=1}^N T_1(B_i)
        \geq N \left({1-u(r)}\right)^{1/\gamma^2}
        e^{-\varepsilon/\gamma-\delta_\alpha}.
    \]
    Taking logarithms and rearranging,
    \[
    \begin{aligned}
        \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}
        &\geq \log N - \delta_\alpha
        + \frac{1}{\gamma^2}\log(1-u(r)), \\
        \varepsilon
        &\geq \gamma\left({\log N-\delta_\alpha}\right)
        + \frac{1}{\gamma}\log(1-u(r)).
    \end{aligned}
    \]
    Similarly, summing the second lower bound gives
    \[
        1 \geq \sum_{i=1}^N T_1(B_i)
        \geq N\left({1-e^{\gamma^2\varepsilon+\gamma\delta_\alpha}u(r)^{\gamma^2}}\right),
    \]
    hence
    \[
        e^{\gamma^2\varepsilon+\gamma\delta_\alpha}u(r)^{\gamma^2}
        \geq \frac{N-1}{N}.
    \]
    Taking logarithms and dividing by $\gamma^2$ yields
    \[
        \varepsilon \geq
        \frac{1}{\gamma^2}\log\frac{N-1}{N}
        -\frac{\delta_\alpha}{\gamma}-\log u(r).
    \]

    In both cases, taking the supremum over $\left\{{r \in (0, \Delta/2): 0 < u(r) < 1}\right\}$ gives the final bounds.

label: def:teaching-dim
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:teaching-dim}
    Let $\cX$ be an instance space, and let $\cH \subseteq \left\{{0,1}\right\}^{\cX}$ be a hypothesis class over $\cX$.
    For a hypothesis $h \in \cH$, a set $T \subseteq \cX \times \left\{{0,1}\right\}$ is called a \textit{teaching set} for $h$ if $h$ is consistent with $T$ and no other hypothesis $h' \in \cH \setminus \{h\}$ is consistent with $T$.
    Let $\mathcal{T}(h)$ denote the collection of all teaching sets for $h$.
    The \textit{teaching dimension} of $\cH$ is defined as
    \[
        \mathrm{TD}(\cH)
        \coloneqq
        \max_{h \in \cH}
        \min_{T \in \mathcal{T}(h)}
        |T|.
    \]

name: Teaching dimension

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h_0 \in \cH$ have a teaching set $T_0$. A teaching set size is upper-bounded by the teaching dimension, hence $|T_0| \leq \tau$. Similarly, let $R_i$ be teaching sets for $h_i$, with $|R_i| \leq \tau$ as well.
    Construct the common unlearning request as $\tau+1$ copies of $T_0$: $U = \uplus_{i=1}^{\tau+1} T_0$, so
    $|U| \leq \tau (\tau + 1)$. Set $S_i = R_i \cup U$, so $|S_i| \leq \tau (\tau + 2)$.

    Consider first the hypothesis $h_0$. On $S_i$, it errs only on the retain part $R_i$. $U$ consists of copies of $T_0$, which is perfectly fitted by $h_0$ by construction. As $|R_i| \leq \tau$, $h_0$ can make at most $\tau$ mistakes on it. On the other hand, $h_i \neq h_0$ perfectly fits the retain part $R_i$. However, on each of the $\tau+1$ copies of $T_0$ in $U$, it must make at least one mistake, as $h_0$ is the only hypothesis that perfectly fits $U$. Therefore, $h_i$ makes at least $\tau + 1$ mistakes on $S_i$. Combining these two results, we obtain that $\mathcal{A}(S_i) = h_0$ for any $i \in [N]$. The retrained targets are $\mathcal{A}(S_i \setminus U) = \mathcal{A}(R_i) = h_i$, again by the teaching set property.

    Therefore, the above implies that $N$ different datasets exactly collide under any ERM $\mathcal{A}$, but are strictly separated under retraining.

title: Proof
body_md:
\label{app:proof-thresholds}
For a realizable sample \(S\), write
\(n(S)\coloneqq \max\{x:(x,-1)\in S\}\) and
\(p(S)\coloneqq \min\{x:(x,+1)\in S\}\). Thus
\(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S)=\left({n(S)+p(S)}\right)/2\).

We first prove the lower bound. Let
\(
    U = \cup_{i=1}^m \left\{{
        (-c+1, +1)
    }\right\}
\)
be the deletion multiset.
Define the following multisets:
\[
S_1
=
U \cup 
\left\{{
    (-c, -1), (-c+1, +1)
}\right\}
\qquad
S_2
=
U \cup
\left\{{
    (-c, -1), (c, +1)
}\right\}.
\]
Pad each dataset with \(n-m-2\) additional copies of \((-c,-1)\).
Both full samples have largest negative example \(-c\) and smallest
positive example \(-c+1\), so
\(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_1)=\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_2)=-c+\frac12\). 
After deleting \(U\),
however, \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_1\setminus U)=-c+\frac12\) and
\(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_2\setminus U)=0\).
Hence, \((S_1,S_2,U)\) is a $(2, m, c-\frac12, |\cdot|;0,0)$-shared-deletion example.

It remains to show that no larger separation is possible. Consider any
shared-deletion example \((S_1,S_2,U)\) with \(|U|\le m\). Put
\(a_i=n(S_i)\), \(b_i=p(S_i)\), \(a_i'=n(S_i\setminus U)\), and
\(b_i'=p(S_i\setminus U)\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). Since
\(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_1)=\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_2)\), we have \(a_1+b_1=a_2+b_2\).
Assume without loss of generality that
\(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_2\setminus U)\ge \mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_1\setminus U)\).
Then
\[
\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_2\setminus U)-\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_1\setminus U)
\le
\frac{c-b_2}{2}
+
\frac{a_1+c}{2}.
\]
If \(b_2'=b_2\), then the first term is unnecessary and the bound is at
most \((a_1+c)/2\le c-\frac12\), since \(a_1\le c-1\). Similarly, if
\(a_1'=a_1\), then the bound is at most
\((c-b_2)/2\le c-\frac12\), since \(b_2\ge -c+1\).

It remains to consider the case \(b_2'>b_2\) and \(a_1'<a_1\). Then
\(U\) must contain \((b_2,+1)\), so \((b_2,+1)\in S_1\) and hence
\(b_2\ge b_1\). Also \(U\) must contain \((a_1,-1)\), so
\((a_1,-1)\in S_2\) and hence \(a_1\le a_2\). Together with
\(a_1+b_1=a_2+b_2\), these inequalities imply \(a_1=a_2\) and
\(b_1=b_2\).
Thus, writing \(a=a_1=a_2\) and \(b=b_1=b_2\),
\[
\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_2\setminus U)-\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{th}}(S_1\setminus U)
\le
\frac{a+c}{2}+\frac{c-b}{2}
=
c-\frac{b-a}{2}
\le
c-\frac12,
\]
because \(a,b\in\mathcal X_c\) and \(a<b\). Thus the largest admissible
separation in a \((2,m,\Delta,\left| {\cdot} \right|;0,0)\)-s.d.e. is
\(\Delta=c-\frac12\).

title: Proof
body_md:
For each \(i\in\{1,2\}\), write the multiset \(S_i\) in sorted order as
\(x_1^{(i)}\le \cdots \le x_n^{(i)}\).

We first consider the even case \(n=2r\), with \(r\in\mathbb N\). Since
\((S_1,S_2,U)\) is a shared-deletion example, the original medians coincide;
write \(M=\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i)
=(x_r^{(i)}+x_{r+1}^{(i)})/2\), so
\(x_r^{(i)}\le M\le x_{r+1}^{(i)}\), for \(i\in\{1,2\}\).

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Case \(m=1\). Write \(U=\left\{{u}\right\}\). Suppose first that \(u<M\).
    Then deletion removes a point from the left half of each dataset, so
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}\left({S_i\setminus U}\right)=x_{r+1}^{(i)}\). Since
    \(x_{r+1}^{(i)}=2M-x_r^{(i)}\), \(x_r^{(i)}\ge -c\), and
    \(x_{r+1}^{(i)}\le c\), we have
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}\left({S_i\setminus U}\right)\in
    \left[{M,\min\left\{{c,2M+c}\right\}}\right]\), an interval of length at most \(c\). The case
    \(u>M\) is analogous and gives
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}\left({S_i\setminus U}\right)\in
    \left[{\max\left\{{-c,2M-c}\right\},M}\right]\), again an interval of length at most \(c\).
    Finally, if \(u=M\), then necessarily \(x_r^{(i)}=x_{r+1}^{(i)}=M\), so
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}\left({S_i\setminus U}\right)=M\). Hence, in all cases,
    \(\left| {\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_1\setminus U)
    -\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_2\setminus U)} \right|\le c\).

    This bound is tight. Take \(S_1=\left\{{-c,0,\ldots,0}\right\}\), with \(2r-1\)
    copies of \(0\), and \(S_2=\left\{{-c,\ldots,-c,c,\ldots,c}\right\}\), with \(r\)
    copies of \(-c\) and \(r\) copies of \(c\). Both medians are \(0\).
    Removing the common multiset \(U=\left\{{-c}\right\}\) gives post-deletion medians
    \(0\) and \(c\), so the separation is \(c\). Therefore the largest
    admissible separation in a \((2,1,\Delta,\left| {\cdot} \right|;0,0)\)-s.d.e.
    is \(\Delta=c\).

    \item Case \(m=2\). Write \(U=\left\{{u,v}\right\}\), with \(u\le v\). Consider first
    \(u\le v<M\). Then both deleted points lie below the common median, so
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)
    =(x_{r+1}^{(i)}+x_{r+2}^{(i)})/2
    =M+(x_{r+2}^{(i)}-x_r^{(i)})/2\). Since
    \(-c\le x_r^{(i)}\le x_{r+2}^{(i)}\le c\), we get
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)\in
    \left[{M,\min\left\{{c,M+c}\right\}}\right]\), an interval of length at most \(c\). The case
    \(M<u\le v\) is analogous.

    It remains to consider \(u\le M\le v\). Write the remaining points as
    \(y_1^{(i)}\le\cdots\le y_{2r-2}^{(i)}\), so that
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)
    =(y_{r-1}^{(i)}+y_r^{(i)})/2\). If \(u<M<v\), one point is deleted from
    each side of the median, so \(y_{r-1}^{(i)}\le M\le y_r^{(i)}\). If a
    deleted value equals \(M\), then \(M\) is a sample value, hence
    \(x_r^{(i)}=x_{r+1}^{(i)}=M\), and the same bracketing still holds.
    Therefore
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)\in
    \left[{(M-c)/2,(M+c)/2}\right]\), again an interval of length \(c\). Thus, in all
    cases,
    \(\left| {\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_1\setminus U)
    -\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_2\setminus U)} \right|\le c\).

    The bound is tight. For \(r\ge2\), take
    \(S_1=\left\{{-c,\ldots,-c,0,\ldots,0}\right\}\), with \(r-1\) copies of \(-c\) and
    \(r+1\) copies of \(0\), and \(S_2=\left\{{0,\ldots,0,c,\ldots,c}\right\}\), with
    \(r+1\) copies of \(0\) and \(r-1\) copies of \(c\). Both medians are \(0\).
    Deleting \(U=\left\{{0,0}\right\}\) gives post-deletion medians \(-c/2\) and \(c/2\),
    so the separation is \(c\). Hence the largest admissible separation
    in a \((2,2,\Delta,\left| {\cdot} \right|;0,0)\)-s.d.e. is \(\Delta=c\).

    \item Case \(3\le m\le n-1\). Consider again the datasets from the previous
    case, and take \(U=\left\{{0,0,0}\right\}\). Then
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_1\setminus U)=-c\) and
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_2\setminus U)=c\), so the separation is
    \(2c\). This achieves the trivial upper bound \(2c\). Since an s.d.e.
    allows \(|U|\le m\), this construction is admissible for every
    \(m\ge3\). Hence the largest admissible separation in a
    \((2,m,\Delta,\left| {\cdot} \right|;0,0)\)-s.d.e. is \(\Delta=2c\) for all
    \(3\le m\le n-1\).
\end{enumerate}

Now consider the odd case \(n=2r-1\), with \(r\in\mathbb N\). For each
\(i\in\{1,2\}\), the median is
\(M=\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i)=x_r^{(i)}\).

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Case \(m=1\). Write \(U=\left\{{u}\right\}\). If \(u<M\), then
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)
    =(x_r^{(i)}+x_{r+1}^{(i)})/2=(M+x_{r+1}^{(i)})/2\), and hence
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)\in\left[{M,(M+c)/2}\right]\).
    Similarly, if \(u>M\), then
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)\in\left[{(M-c)/2,M}\right]\). Finally,
    if \(u=M\), then
    \(\mathcal{A}_c^{\mathrm{med}}(S_i\setminus U)
    =(x_{r-1}^{(i)}+x_{r+1}^{(i)})/2\in\left[{(M-c)/2,(M+c)/2}\right]\). In all cases,
    the two post-deletion medians lie in a common interval of length at most
    \(c\), so their separation is at most \(c\).

    This bound is tight. For \(r\ge2\), take
    \(S_1=\left\{{-c,\ldots,-c,c,\ldots,c}\right\}\), with \(r-1\) copies of \(-c\) and
    \(r\) copies of \(c\), and \(S_2=\left\{{c,\ldots,c}\right\}\), with \(2r-1\) copies
    of \(c\). Both medians are \(c\). Removing the common multiset \(U=\left\{{c}\right\}\)
    gives post-deletion medians \(0\) and \(c\), so the separation is \(c\).
    Therefore the largest admissible separation in a
    \((2,1,\Delta,\left| {\cdot} \right|;0,0)\)-s.d.e. is \(\Delta=c\).

    \item Case \(2\le m\le n-1\). Take
    \(S_1=\left\{{-c,\ldots,-c,0,\ldots,0}\right\}\), with \(r-1\) copies of \(-c\) and
    \(r\) copies of \(0\), and \(S_2=\left\{{0,\ldots,0,c,\ldots,c}\right\}\), with \(r\)
    copies of \(0\) and \(r-1\) copies of \(c\). Both medians are \(0\).
    Deleting \(U=\left\{{0,0}\right\}\) gives post-deletion medians \(-c\) and \(c\), so
    the separation is \(2c\), which is the trivial upper bound. Since an
    s.d.e. allows \(|U|\le m\), this construction is admissible for
    every \(2\le m\le n-1\). Hence the largest admissible separation in a
    \((2,m,\Delta,\left| {\cdot} \right|;0,0)\)-s.d.e. is \(\Delta=2c\) for all such \(m\).
\end{enumerate}

body_md:
\label{app:proof-svm}
We write the construction first for odd \(n\). Let \(q=(n-1)/2\), and define
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_\rho
&=
\{(\rho e_1,+1)\},\\
S_{1,\rho}
&=
U_\rho
\biguplus_{j=1}^{q}
\{(-\rho(e_1+e_2),-1),(\rho(e_1+e_2),+1)\},\\
S_{2,\rho}
&=
U_\rho
\biguplus_{j=1}^{q}
\{(-\rho(e_1-e_2),-1),(\rho(e_1-e_2),+1)\},
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\uplus\) denotes multiset union. Thus each dataset contains one copy of
\((\rho e_1,+1)\), together with \(q\) copies of each of the two remaining
labeled points, and therefore has size \(1+2q=n\). 
For even \(n\), the same construction is obtained by taking
\(q=(n-2)/2\) and adding one extra duplicate of any nondeleted point; duplicates
do not change the hard-margin SVM constraints. 
All points in
\(S_{1,\rho}\cup S_{2,\rho}\) lie in the unit ball because
\(\left\lVert\rho e_1\right\rVert_2=\rho\le1\) and
\(\left\lVert\rho(e_1\pm e_2)\right\rVert_2=\rho\sqrt{2}\le1\).

We first compute the SVM on the full datasets. For \(S_{1,\rho}\), the
margin constraints are
\[
\left\langle{w},{\rho e_1}\right\rangle\ge1,
\qquad
\left\langle{w},{\rho(e_1+e_2)}\right\rangle\ge1,
\]
or equivalently \(w_1\ge1/\rho\) and \(w_1+w_2\ge1/\rho\). The first
inequality implies \(\left\lVertw\right\rVert_2\ge |w_1|\ge1/\rho\), while
\(\rho^{-1}e_1\) satisfies both inequalities with norm \(1/\rho\). Thus
\(\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}(S_{1,\rho})=\rho^{-1}e_1\). The same
argument for \(S_{2,\rho}\), whose nonredundant constraints are
\(w_1\ge1/\rho\) and \(w_1-w_2\ge1/\rho\), gives
\(\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}(S_{2,\rho})=\rho^{-1}e_1\).

After deleting \(U_\rho\), the first retained sample consists of the
two labeled points \((-\rho(e_1+e_2),-1)\) and
\((\rho(e_1+e_2),+1)\). Its hard-margin SVM is the minimum-norm vector
\(w\) such that \(\left\langle{w},{\rho(e_1+e_2)}\right\rangle\ge1\). By Cauchy--Schwarz, the
unique minimizer is parallel to \(e_1+e_2\) and satisfies the constraint
with equality, hence
\[
\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}(S_{1,\rho}\setminus U_\rho)
=
\frac{1}{2\rho}(e_1+e_2).
\]
Similarly,
\[
\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}(S_{2,\rho}\setminus U_\rho)
=
\frac{1}{2\rho}(e_1-e_2).
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\lVert
\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}(S_{1,\rho}\setminus U_\rho)
-
\mathcal{A}_d^{\mathrm{svm}}(S_{2,\rho}\setminus U_\rho)
\right\rVert_2
=
\frac{1}{\rho}.
\]
Since \(\rho>0\) can be taken arbitrarily small, for every \(\Delta>0\)
the construction gives a \((2,1,\Delta,\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_2;0,0)\)-s.d.e. by choosing \(\rho\) sufficiently small. Since \(|U_\rho|=1\le m\),
the same construction gives a \((2,m,\Delta,\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_2;0,0)\)-s.d.e.
for every \(1\le m\le n-1\).

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $s$ and $u$ with $u\subseteq s$ and $|u|\le m$. Throughout, write
    $\@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right)_{s,u}(\cdot) \coloneqq \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right)(\cdot\mid S=s,U=u)$ and
    $p(w\mid s,u) \coloneqq \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right)_{s,u}(W=w)$ for the law of the retraining target.
    
    Since $(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{\bar{A}})$ is $(\alpha,\varepsilon)$-RU, the laws of
    $\overline W$ and $W^\emptyset$ under $\mathbb P_{s,u}$ satisfy
    $D_\alpha(\overline W\,\|\,W^\emptyset)\le\varepsilon$. For fixed
    $w\in\mathcal W$, applying~\Cref{lem:renyi-event-transfer} to the event
    $A_w\coloneqq\{x\in\mathcal W: x\ne w\}$ gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lem42-transfer}
        \mathbb P_{s,u}\big(\overline W\ne w\big)
        \le e^{\gamma\varepsilon}\,
        \mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset\ne w\big)^{\gamma}.
    \end{equation}
    
    Multiplying~\eqref{eq:lem42-transfer} by $p(w\mid s,u)$, summing over $w$, and
    using Jensen's inequality, since $x\mapsto x^\gamma$ is concave for
    $0<\gamma<1$, gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lem42-jensen}
        \sum_{w\in\mathcal W}p(w\mid s,u)\,\mathbb P_{s,u}\big(\overline W\ne w\big)
        \le e^{\gamma\varepsilon}\Big(\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}p(w\mid s,u)\,
        \mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset\ne w\big)\Big)^{\gamma}.
    \end{equation}
    Since $\overline W \perp\!\!\!\perp W\mid
    (S,U)$, the left-hand side equals $\mathbb P_{s,u}(\overline W\ne W)$.
    
    We now bound the term inside the parentheses.
    Let $W_1,W_2$ be independent copies of $W$ under $\mathbb P_{s,u}$, that is,
    independent runs of $\mathcal{A}(s\setminus u)$, and let
    $W^\emptyset_2 \coloneqq \mathcal{\bar{A}}(W_2,\emptyset)$. Expanding over the law of the
    target from which $W^\emptyset$ is generated,
    \begin{gather}
    \begin{aligned}\label{eq:lem42-coupling}
        \sum_{w\in\mathcal W}p(w\mid s,u)\,\mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset\ne w\big)
        &=\sum_{w,w'\in\mathcal W}p(w\mid s,u)\,p(w'\mid s,u)\,
        \mathbb P\big(W^\emptyset\ne w\mid W=w'\big) \\
        &=\mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset_2\ne W_1\big).
    \end{aligned}
    \end{gather}
    
    Since $\{W^\emptyset_2\ne W_1\}\subseteq\{W^\emptyset_2\ne W_2\}\cup\{W_1\ne W_2\}$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lem42-split}
        \mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset_2\ne W_1\big)
        \le\mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset_2\ne W_2\big)
        +\mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W_1\ne W_2\big).
    \end{equation}
    
    It remains to bound the matched term.
    Since $W^\emptyset$ depends on $(S,U)$ only through $W$, $(d_0,\Gamma)$-utility
    gives
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:lem42-matched}
        \mathbb P_{s,u}\big(W^\emptyset_2\ne W_2\big)
        =\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}p(w\mid s,u)\,
        \mathbb P\big(\mathcal{\bar{A}}(w,\emptyset)\ne w\big)\le\eta .
    \end{equation}
    
    Combining (\ref{eq:lem42-jensen})--(\ref{eq:lem42-matched}),
    \[
        \mathbb P_{s,u}\big(\overline W\ne W\big)
        \le e^{\gamma\varepsilon}\big(\eta+\mathbb P_{s,u}(W_1\ne W_2)\big)^{\gamma}
        \le e^{\gamma\varepsilon}\big(\eta+\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}\big)^{\gamma}.
    \]
    Taking the supremum over $(s,u)$, and using $\beta_{\mathrm{un}}\le1$, gives
    $\beta_{\mathrm{un}}\le\bar\beta$. The two error sources are visible in the
    bound: $\eta$ accounts for the empty-request map moving the target,
    $\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}$ for the randomness of the learner, and the factor
    $e^{\gamma\varepsilon}(\cdot)^{\gamma}$ for approximate unlearning. In
    particular, for deterministic $\mathcal{A}$, $\Delta_{\mathcal{A}}=0$ and
    $\beta_{\mathrm{un}}\le e^{\gamma\varepsilon}\eta^{\gamma}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove the memorization lower bound, we start from the result of~\Cref{pp:information-lb} and will bound the term,
    \[
        I \left(
            W_{\pi(i)}; \overline{W}_{\pi(i)} \mid
            W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right).
    \]
    Assuming the model space \( \mathcal{W} \) is discrete and finite, we have that,
    \begin{gather}
    \begin{aligned}
        I \left(
            W_{\pi(i)}; \overline{W}_{\pi(i)} \mid
            W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right)
        &=
        H \left(
            W_{\pi(i)} |  W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right)
        -
        H \left(
            W_{\pi(i)} |  \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}, W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right) \\
        &\overset{(a)}{\geq}
        H \left(
            W_{\pi(i)} |  W_{\pi(<i)}, U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right)
        -
        H \left(
            W_{\pi(i)} |  \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}
        \right),
    \end{aligned}
    \end{gather}
    where $(a)$ uses that conditioning reduces entropy.

    By Fano's inequality applied to the pair
    \[
        \left(
            W_{\pi(i)},\,
            \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}
        \right),
    \]
    we get
    \[
        H\left(
            W_{\pi(i)}
            \mid
            \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}
        \right)
        \leq
        h(P_{e,\pi(i)})
        +
        P_{e,\pi(i)}\log(|\mathcal W|-1)
        =:
        F(P_{e,\pi(i)})  
        ,
    \]
    where
    \[
        P_{e,\pi(i)}
        \coloneqq
        \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right){
            \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}\neq W_{\pi(i)}
        }.
    \]
    Moreover,
    \[
        P_{e,\pi(i)}
        =
        \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{E}\left(\mathbb{E}\right)_{S,U_{\pi(i)}}
        \left[
        \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{P}\right){
            \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}\neq W_{\pi(i)}
            \mid S,U_{\pi(i)}
        }
        \right]
        \leq
        \@ifnextchar\bgroup\mathbb{E}\left(\mathbb{E}\right)_{S,U_{\pi(i)}}[\beta_{\mathrm{un}}]
        =
        \beta_{\mathrm{un}}
        \leq
        \bar\beta .
    \]
    The function $F$ is increasing on $[0, 1 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal W|}]$, since
    $F'(p) = \log\frac{(1-p)(|\mathcal W|-1)}{p} \geq 0$ there, and it attains its maximum
    $\log|\mathcal W|$ at $p = 1 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal W|}$. Hence, with
    $\tilde\beta \coloneqq \min\{\bar\beta,\, 1 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal W|}\}$, we have
    $F(P_{e,\pi(i)}) \leq F(\tilde\beta)$: by monotonicity if $\bar\beta \leq 1 - \frac{1}{|\mathcal W|}$,
    and by maximality otherwise. Hence, 
    \[
        H\left(
            W_{\pi(i)}
            \mid
            \overline{W}_{\pi(i)}
        \right)
        \le
        h(\tilde\beta) + \tilde\beta\log(|\mathcal W|-1).  
    \]
    Therefore,
    \[
        I\left(
            W_{\pi(i)};\overline{W}_{\pi(i)}
            \mid
            W_{\pi(<i)},U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right)
        \ge
        H\left(
            W_{\pi(i)}
            \mid
            W_{\pi(<i)},U_{\pi(\le i)}
        \right)
        -
        h(\tilde\beta)  
        -
        \tilde\beta\log(|\mathcal W|-1).  
    \]
    Summing over \(i=1,\ldots,K\) and using~\Cref{pp:information-lb} gives the claim.

title: Proof
body_md:
Partition \(\left[{N}\right]\) into \(n\) consecutive bins
    \[
        B_j=\left\{{(j-1)q+1,\ldots,jq}\right\},
        \qquad j\in\left[{n}\right],
    \]
    where \(q=N/n\). Draw \(x_j\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_j)\) independently, and set
    \[
        y_j=\mathds{1}\left\{{j\ge m}\right\}.
    \]
    Let
    \[
        S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)).
    \]
    Since the bins are ordered, every negative example lies to the left of
    every positive example, so \(S\) is realizable by a threshold. By the
    canonical tie-breaking rule, the ERM output on the full sample is
    \[
        \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{ERM}}(S)=h_{x_m}.
    \]

    For each \(i\in\left[{m}\right]\), define the deletion request
    \[
        U_i
        =
        \left\{{(x_j,0):1\le j\le m-i}\right\}
        \cup
        \left\{{(x_j,1):m\le j\le m+i-1}\right\}.
    \]
    The first set has size \(m-i\), the second has size \(i\), and hence
    \(\left| {U_i} \right|=m\). Since \(n\ge2m\), the point \(x_{m+i}\) exists. After deleting
    \(U_i\), the leftmost remaining positive example is \(x_{m+i}\). Therefore
    \[
        W_i
        \coloneqq
        \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{ERM}}(S\setminus U_i)
        =
        h_{x_{m+i}}.
    \]

    Let \(H_i=(W_{<i},U_{\le i})\). The variables in \(H_i\) reveal only points
    from bins other than \(B_{m+i}\). In particular, the previous retraining
    targets \(W_1,\ldots,W_{i-1}\) reveal
    \(x_{m+1},\ldots,x_{m+i-1}\), all of which are already deleted by \(U_i\).
    Since the \(x_j\)'s are independent across bins,
    \[
        x_{m+i}\mid H_i\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_{m+i}).
    \]
    Distinct threshold locations define distinct hypotheses, so
    \[
        H(W_i\mid H_i)=\log q.
    \]

    Applying~\Cref{thm:information-lb-discrete} and substituting
    \(q\) for each \(i\in\left[{m}\right]\), gives the result. Finally, for the
    bare ERM output, we have \(M\), and
    \(x_m\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_m)\). Hence
    \[
        I(M;S)_{\mathrm{bare}}=H(M)=\log q.
    \]

title: Proof
body_md:
Partition \(\left[{d}\right]\) into \(n\) disjoint blocks
    \[
        B_j=\left\{{(j-1)q+1,\ldots,jq}\right\},
        \qquad j\in\left[{n}\right].
    \]
    Let \(e_a\in\mathbb{R}^d\) denote the \(a\)-th standard basis vector.
    Fix strictly decreasing positive numbers
    \[
        \lambda_1>\lambda_2>\cdots>\lambda_n>0.
    \]
    Draw \(a_j\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_j)\) independently and set
    \[
        z_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,e_{a_j}.
    \]
    Let \(S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\).

    The learner returns
    \[
        \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PCA}}(D)
        =
        e_{\widehat a(D)},
        \qquad
        \widehat a(D)
        \in
        \mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{a\in\left[{d}\right]}
        \sum_{z\in D}\left\langle{e_a},{z}\right\rangle^2,
    \]
    with an arbitrary fixed tie-breaking rule. On the full sample, because
    the \(\lambda_j\)'s are strictly decreasing,
    \[
        M_{\mathrm{bare}}
        =
        \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PCA}}(S)
        =
        e_{a_1}.
    \]

    For \(i\in\left[{m}\right]\), define
    \[
        U_i
        =
        \left\{{z_1,\ldots,z_i}\right\}
        \cup
        \left\{{z_{n-m+i+1},\ldots,z_n}\right\},
    \]
    where the second set is empty when \(i=m\). The first set has size \(i\)
    and the second has size \(m-i\), so \(\left| {U_i} \right|=m\). The assumption
    \(2m\le n\) ensures that these deletions do not remove \(z_{i+1}\).

    After deleting \(U_i\), the largest remaining empirical second moment is
    \(\lambda_{i+1}\), attained uniquely at coordinate \(a_{i+1}\). Hence
    \[
        W_i
        \coloneqq
        \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PCA}}(S\setminus U_i)
        =
        e_{a_{i+1}}.
    \]

    Let \(H_i=(W_{<i},U_{\le i})\). The variables in \(H_i\) reveal
    \(a_1,\ldots,a_i\), possibly some tail coordinates, and
    \(a_2,\ldots,a_i\) through the previous retraining targets. They reveal no
    information about \(a_{i+1}\). Since the blocks are independent,
    \[
        a_{i+1}\mid H_i\sim\mathrm{Unif}(B_{i+1}).
    \]
    Therefore
    \[
        H(W_i\mid H_i)=\log q.
    \]

    Applying the conditional-support Fano argument from
    \Cref{sec:examples-disc}, with \(q\) possible targets per request,
    gives the result. For the bare
    PCA output, \(M=e_{a_1}\), so
    \[
        I(M;S)_{\mathrm{bare}}=H(e_{a_1})=\log q.
    \]

title: Proof
body_md:
The main idea is that, for one-hot inputs, \(\left\langle{w},{e_a}\right\rangle=w_a\)
    for every \(a\in[d]\). Therefore, the ridge objective separates
    into independent one-dimensional problems. For a dataset \(D\),
    its unique minimizer satisfies
    \[\left[{\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{ridge}}(D)}\right]_a=T_a(D)/(N_a(D)+\lambda),\]
    where \(N_a(D)\) is the number of examples with input \(e_a\),
    and \(T_a(D)\) is the sum of their labels. We construct datasets
    with equally many copies of \((e_a,+1)\) and \((e_a,-1)\), so
    all fitted coefficients are zero regardless of \(N_a(D)\).
    Deleting one copy of \((e_a,+1)\) changes the corresponding label
    sum to \(-1\), making the retrained coefficient depend on
    \(N_a(D)\). Accurate unlearning therefore requires retaining
    information about these counts. The remaining examples in the
    construction ensure that the total dataset size stays fixed
    despite this randomness.

    Draw \(C_1,\ldots,C_b\) independently and uniformly from
    \(\left\{{1,2,3}\right\}\). Block \(j\) contains \(C_j\) copies of each of
    \((e_{2j-1},+1)\) and \((e_{2j-1},-1)\), and \(4-C_j\) copies
    of each of \((e_{2j},+1)\) and \((e_{2j},-1)\). Each block
    therefore has eight examples, giving \(n=8b\). Place one copy
    of \((e_{2j-1},+1)\) first in each block, order the remaining
    examples deterministically, and concatenate the blocks to obtain
    \(S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\). Since all label sums are zero,
    \(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{ridge}}(S)=0\).

    For each \(i\in[b]\), let
    \(U_i=\left\{{z_{8(i-1)+1}}\right\}=\left\{{(e_{2i-1},+1)}\right\}\). Both its index
    and value are fixed, so this singleton request reveals nothing
    about \(C_i\). After deletion, there are \(2C_i-1\) examples
    with input \(e_{2i-1}\), with label sum \(-1\), while all other
    label sums remain zero. Thus
    \[
        W_i=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{ridge}}(S\setminus U_i)
        =-\frac{1}{2C_i-1+\lambda}\,e_{2i-1}.
    \]
    The three values of \(C_i\) give three distinct retraining
    models it needs to match. Let \(\mathcal H_i=(W_{<i},U_{\le i})\).
    Previous targets reveal only \(C_1,\ldots,C_{i-1}\), and the
    requests are deterministic. Hence \(C_i\) is still uniformly
    random given \(\mathcal H_i\), so
    \(H(W_i\mid\mathcal H_i)=\log3\). For \(\beta_3<2/3\),
    applying the conditional-support Fano bound from
    \Cref{sec:examples-disc} and \Cref{pp:information-lb} gives
    \[
        I(M;S)
        \ge b\bigl[\log3-h(\beta_3)-\beta_3\log2\bigr]
        =\frac n8\bigl[\log3-h(\beta_3)-\beta_3\log2\bigr].
    \]
    For \(\beta_3=2/3\), the bound follows from nonnegativity.
    Finally, the bare fitted vector is identically zero on this
    distribution, so \(I(M;S)_{\mathrm{bare}}=0\).

title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(r=r_\star\). By definition of \(r_\star\), we have
    \(r^2\le d\) and \(r(m+1)\le n\). Since \(d>4\) and \(n>3m\), we have
    \(r\ge2\).

    We use the first \(r^2\) ambient coordinates as an \(r\times r\)
    matrix.  If \(n>r(m+1)\), we add \(n-r(m+1)\) deterministic dummy
    measurements of the form \((1,0_r,0)\). These impose no constraint
    and do not affect the fitted matrix.

    Draw a uniformly random permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\left[{r}\right]\). For
    each row \(i\in\left[{r}\right]\), include \(m\) indexed copies of the row-sum
    measurement
    \[
        c_i^{(a)}=(i,\mathbf 1_r,r),
        \qquad a\in\left[{m}\right],
    \]
    and one coordinate measurement
    \[
        z_i=(i,e_{\sigma(i)},1).
    \]
    Thus the non-dummy part of the dataset has size \(r(m+1)\). The
    copies are treated as distinct indexed examples, so a deletion
    request may delete all \(m\) row-sum copies in a row.

    We first compute the fitted matrix on the full dataset. Because
    the data are consistent and \(\lambda\to0\), the learner selects,
    among interpolating matrices, one minimizing
    \[
        \sum_{i=1}^r \left\lVertx_i\right\rVert_2.
    \]
    The rows decouple. Fix row \(i\). The constraints are
    \[
        \sum_{\ell=1}^r (x_i)_\ell=r,
        \qquad
        (x_i)_{\sigma(i)}=1.
    \]
    Therefore the remaining \(r-1\) coordinates must sum to \(r-1\). By
    Cauchy--Schwarz,
    \[
        \sum_{\ell\neq\sigma(i)} (x_i)_\ell^2
        \ge
        \frac{(r-1)^2}{r-1}
        =
        r-1,
    \]
    with equality iff all remaining coordinates are equal to \(1\). Hence the
    unique minimum-norm interpolating row is
    \[
        x_i=\mathbf 1_r.
    \]
    This holds for every row, so the full fitted matrix is deterministic:
    \[
        M_{\mathrm{bare}}
        =
        \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{fac}}(S)
        =
        \mathbf 1_r\mathbf 1_r^\top.
    \]

    For each row \(i\in\left[{r}\right]\), define
    \[
        U_i=\left\{{c_i^{(1)},\ldots,c_i^{(m)}}\right\}.
    \]
    This deletion request has size \(m\). After deleting \(U_i\), row \(i\)
    has only the coordinate constraint
    \[
        (x_i)_{\sigma(i)}=1.
    \]
    The unique minimum-\(\ell_2\)-norm row satisfying this constraint is
    \[
        x_i=e_{\sigma(i)}.
    \]
    All other rows still have both their row-sum and coordinate measurements,
    so they remain equal to \(\mathbf 1_r\). Thus
    \(W_i=\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{fac}}(S\setminus U_i)\) is the matrix whose
    \(i\)-th row is \(e_{\sigma(i)}\) and whose other rows are
    \(\mathbf 1_r\). In particular, \(W_i\) reveals exactly \(\sigma(i)\).

    Let $\mathcal H_i = (W_{<i}, U_{\le i})$. The deletion requests themselves are deterministic
    functions of the row index and reveal no information about $\sigma$. After observing
    $W_1, \dots, W_{i-1}$, one knows $\sigma(1), \dots, \sigma(i-1)$. Since $\sigma$ is a uniformly
    random permutation, conditional on this information, $\sigma(i)$ is uniform over the remaining
    $q_i \coloneqq r - i + 1$ columns. Therefore
    \[
        H(W_i \mid \mathcal H_i) = \log q_i .
    \]
    Applying the conditional-support Fano argument from \Cref{sec:examples-disc} with $q_i$ possible
    targets for request $i$, and noting that the last request ($q_r = 1$) has zero conditional entropy
    and zero penalty, we get, with $s = q_i$,
    \[
        I(M;S)
        \geq
        \log(r!) - \sum_{s=2}^{r} \left[{h(\beta_s) + \beta_s \log(s-1)}\right],
    \]
    where we used $\sum_{s=2}^{r} \log s = \log(r!)$.
    Finally, $M$ is deterministic on this distribution, so
    $I(M;S)_{\mathrm{bare}} = 0$.
